opus-5.5.text:
Mostly for practical reasons. During pretraining we sample the number of recurrences randomly, drawing from a heavy-tailed, log-normal Poisson–style distribution. That way the model usually sees a moderate number of iterations but occasionally sees many more. We draw that number once per step and apply it to the whole sequence, because that keeps training simple and hardware-friendly. Every token goes through the same unrolled computation, so you can batch everything densely on the accelerator. You don't have ragged per-token compute, masking headaches, or load imbalance across the sequence.

If you wanted a different depth for each token, you'd need some mechanism to decide that depth, like a router or a halting signal. Those are notoriously finicky to train and add their own losses and hyperparameters. We wanted to see how far you get without any of that machinery, just by making the model robust to being run for a variable number of steps.

What's nice is that you don't lose per-token adaptivity by training this way. Because the model learns to handle arbitrary recurrence counts, at inference you can do per-token adaptive compute zero-shot. For example, you can stop iterating on a token once the latent state converges, measured by something like the KL divergence between successive steps. Then easy tokens exit early and harder ones keep thinking. So uniform recurrence was the simple, scalable choice for pretraining, and the adaptivity comes for free afterwards.

r001.rationale: The response says applying the same recurrence count across the sequence enables dense batching on the accelerator and avoids ragged per-token compute, conveying that parallel execution across tokens uses equal computation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question we get a lot, because the whole point of the architecture is that you can vary the amount of compute per token at test time. So why not do that during training too?

The honest answer is that it's mostly about simplicity and hardware efficiency. When you're pretraining at scale, you want every sequence in the batch to look the same to the GPU. If I say token one gets four recurrence steps and token two gets thirty-two, now I've got ragged computation, I need masking or some kind of early-exit bookkeeping, and the kernels get much less efficient. It's a real engineering headache, and when you're already fighting for every bit of throughput on a fixed compute budget, that's a hard sell.

So what we do instead is sample the number of recurrence steps per sequence, not per token. Each training sequence draws a step count from a distribution, we use something like a log-normal Poisson, and then the whole sequence runs for that many iterations. Over the course of training, the model sees a lot of different depths. That's really what matters. It learns to make progress on the latent state at every step, and it learns that it may be asked to stop at any point, so it can't rely on, say, step twelve always being there. And that turns out to be enough. At inference time you can then pick a step count per token, or use a convergence criterion to stop early, and the model behaves sensibly even though it never saw per-token variation in training.

The other piece is that we don't actually have a good training signal for how many steps a given token "should" get. Nobody labels that. You could try to learn a halting policy, in the spirit of adaptive computation time, but those approaches have historically been finicky to train, and we were worried about adding that complexity to a run we were only going to get one shot at. The per-sequence sampling gives you most of the benefit at essentially zero cost.

And honestly, I think the fact that it transfers is one of the more interesting findings. The model generalizes to a regime of compute allocation it was never explicitly trained on, which suggests the recurrence is learning something genuinely iterative rather than just memorizing a fixed-depth circuit.

r001.rationale: The response explains that giving different tokens different recurrence counts creates ragged computation and makes GPU kernels less efficient, so training uses the same step count across a sequence.

astra-6.text:
Mostly for simplicity and training efficiency. During pretraining, we process all the tokens in a sequence in parallel, and using the same number of recurrence steps lets us keep that computation uniform. If each token had its own step count, we’d need a way to decide when each token stops, and then handle that irregular computation efficiently.

That doesn’t mean every token needs the same amount of computation. It’s a simplifying choice for pretraining. At inference, when you’re generating tokens one at a time, there’s a much more natural opportunity to vary the number of steps and spend more computation where it’s useful.

r001.rationale: The response says equal step counts keep computation uniform and that per-token counts would require handling irregular computation efficiently. It presents this as a simplifying efficiency choice, not as a requirement imposed by parallelizing computation across tokens.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is computational efficiency during training. If you use the same number of recurrent steps for every token, you can process all the tokens in parallel, which fits very naturally into the way we train language models on GPUs. If each token takes a different number of steps, that becomes much harder to batch efficiently.

That doesn’t mean the number of steps has to be fixed forever. You can vary it between training examples or batches while keeping it uniform across the tokens in a sequence. And at inference time, when you’re generating one token at a time, you have more flexibility to adapt the amount of computation.

r001.rationale: The response says using the same number of recurrent steps for every token lets the tokens be processed in parallel, while differing step counts make batching harder.
